title: The Apology He Hates
subtitle: After Always · Chapter 19 of 40
content:
It turned out Severus Snape could flirt.

He was simply malicious about it.

For three days after Hogsmeade, he behaved as though nothing had changed while changing everything by half an inch.

He stood closer when reading over my shoulder.

He passed ingredients directly into my hand instead of setting them down.

He said “good morning” before insulting my filing system.

Once, while I was bent over a lower cabinet, he murmured, “Your observational skills appear compromised from that angle.”

I hit my head on the shelf.

He looked unbearably pleased.

“This is your fault,” I said, rubbing my scalp.

“Your spatial awareness is not my responsibility.”

“You distracted me.”

“With a factual statement.”

“You're awful.”

“And yet.”

And yet.

Two words nearly undid me.

The problem with warmth from Snape was that it came in such small amounts I noticed every degree.

Which meant I also noticed when it vanished.

The letter arrived after lunch.

No official seal. No signature on the outside. Snape recognized the handwriting and went pale.

He opened it.

Read three lines.

Folded it.

Then became impossible.

Not ordinary impossible.

Sharp.

He criticized everything I touched. My knife angle. My labels. My pronunciation of an obscure ingredient name. When I asked if he wanted to stop work for the day, he accused me of condescension.

I tolerated it for an hour.

Then he said, “If your concentration is so easily disrupted by personal curiosity, perhaps you are unsuited to professional work.”

I set down the jar.

“No.”

He looked up.

“You do not get to do that.”

“Do what?”

“Turn whatever is in that letter into an excuse to make me bleed.”

His face changed.

“How melodramatic.”

“There. That.”

“You are imagining injury because you dislike criticism.”

“I can take criticism. You've been criticizing me since we met. This is different.”

His eyes went cold.

“You flatter yourself.”

The words hit harder than they should have.

He saw it.

And then, because fear makes some people reach and others strike, Snape chose the blade.

“You mistake proximity for importance,” he said.

Silence.

I felt something inside me go very quiet.

“All right,” I said.

His face flickered.

I took off my dragon-hide gloves and set them on the table.

“You're right about one thing. I am too distracted to work safely.”

I packed my notes.

Snape watched.

“What are you doing?”

“Leaving.”

“You are contracted until—”

“For the day.”

His mouth tightened.

“I did not dismiss you.”

“I don't require dismissal.”

That landed.

Good.

I hated wanting it to.

I left before he could say anything else.

The corridor blurred for the first several minutes, which I blamed on torch smoke because I had pride.

I spent the afternoon in the library reviewing contamination law and understanding none of it.

At dinner, Snape did not appear.

At eight, someone knocked on my door.

I knew who it was before opening.

He stood in the corridor without robes, wearing the same black coat from Spinner's End. His hair was damp. He held no umbrella.

I folded my arms.

“What?”

Snape's face looked miserable.

Good, a mean part of me thought.

Then I hated that too.

“I owe you an apology.”

The words sounded physically painful.

I said nothing.

He continued.

“What I said was cruel.”

“Yes.”

“It was also false.”

My chest tightened.

He looked at the floor for one second, then forced himself to meet my eyes.

“You do not mistake proximity for importance.”

I waited.

Snape's jaw flexed.

“You are important.”

There.

No poetry.

No softness around the edges.

Just truth extracted at cost.

I could have rescued him from the moment.

I did not.

“And?” I asked.

His eyes flashed with irritation.

I almost smiled.

“And I used knowledge of your… regard for me as a weapon because I was angry about something unrelated.”

“Yes.”

“That was contemptible.”

“It was.”

“You need not agree so enthusiastically.”

“You need not be so accurate.”

His mouth twitched.

Not enough.

I leaned against the doorframe.

“Why did the letter upset you?”

His face closed.

I held up a hand.

“You don't have to tell me. But if you're asking me to trust that this won't happen every time something scares you, I need to know you understand what happened.”

A long silence.

“The letter was from Lucius Malfoy.”

That I had not expected.

“From prison?”

“Awaiting formal sentencing.”

“What did he want?”

“To remind me of several things we did together.”

The words were flat.

“To threaten you?”

“No. Worse.”

I waited.

“To forgive me.”

I stared.

Snape laughed once without humor.

“He wrote that we had both been used by a madman. That our mistakes should remain buried with him. That old friends ought not testify against one another.”

“Ah.”

“Yes.”

“You're testifying.”

“Yes.”

“And he knows it.”

“Yes.”

I understood now.

Lucius had reached through years of complicity and offered Snape the easiest lie: none of it was truly ours.

No wonder he had been furious.

No wonder he had turned it on himself.

It still did not excuse what he did to me.

Both can be true.

“Did you answer?”

“No.”

“Will you?”

“Yes.”

“What will you say?”

“That he may call his choices whatever he likes. I will call mine mine.”

I exhaled.

“That sounds like you.”

“It is unfortunate.”

I looked at him.

“I'm still angry.”

“You should be.”

“I'm not going to pretend the apology fixed it immediately.”

“I did not expect you to.”

“And if you do that again, I will leave again.”

His face tightened.

“Permanently?”

There was fear beneath the question.

I let myself see it without exploiting it.

“If it becomes a pattern, yes.”

He flinched almost invisibly.

“Understood.”

I softened by a fraction.

“Do you want tea?”

His eyebrows rose.

“Do not read too much into it.”

“I would never.”

I stepped aside.

He entered.

My quarters were temporary and impersonal. A bed. A desk. Two chairs. Books everywhere because I had failed to unpack them properly.

Snape looked around.

“You live like this voluntarily?”

“You came here to apologize. Don't ruin it.”

He sat.

I made tea.

Mine with milk. His black.

When I handed him the cup, our fingers touched.

He did not use the moment to make anything easier.

Neither did I.

We talked about Lucius.

Not the whole history. Enough.

Snape told me they had been friends once, if friendship was the right word for alliances built on ambition and ideology. Lucius had been older. Wealthier. Certain. The kind of person a poor half-blood boy in secondhand robes might mistake for proof that belonging could be earned if he chose the correct side.

“That does not excuse me,” Snape said.

“I know.”

“You do not need to keep saying that.”

“You keep expecting me to.”

His gaze dropped.

“Perhaps.”

The tea cooled.

At some point, our anger became tired instead of sharp.

At the door, Snape stopped.

“I am sorry,” he said again.

This time, no explanation followed.

I believed him.

“Thank you.”

He nodded.

Then he left.

The next morning, he did not flirt.

Neither did I.

We worked carefully around the bruise between us.

At noon, he handed me a jar without setting it down first.

Our fingers touched.

He waited.

I took it.

That was not forgiveness all at once.

It was something better.

The real test of the apology came the next day.

Lucius's second letter arrived at breakfast.

Severus read it once and went pale with anger. I watched every old defense rise: the tightening jaw, the cold eyes, the urge to turn fear into a weapon before anyone could use it against him.

He folded the letter.

Then he looked at me.

“I am in a foul mood,” he said.

“Accurate.”

“I am likely to be unpleasant company.”

“Also accurate.”

“I would prefer an hour alone before we work.”

I stared.

His expression darkened. “Why are you looking at me like that?”

“Because yesterday you sliced me open with three sentences rather than say you were frightened.”

“I was not frightened.”

“You're doing so well. Don't ruin it now.”

His nostrils flared.

Then, astonishingly, he closed his eyes and corrected himself.

“I was angry,” he said. “And frightened. I remain angry. I would still like an hour.”

“Take two.”

His eyes opened.

“No punishment?”

“For asking for space?”

A long pause.

“Some people interpret it that way.”

“I don't.”

He nodded once.

When he returned ninety minutes later, he brought tea.

The apology, I realized, was not the sentence. It was the changed behavior after it.
